en: Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, composed by Dharma Master Huìjìng.

Now, as for the True Doctrine (Buddhism): its profound essence is so wondrous that it transcends the realm of names and expressions; its perfect enlightenment is so subtle and concentrated that it dwells loftily beyond all forms and images.
Beyond the constraints [of conventional categories], one seeks the nature and characteristics [of reality]. Yet, the two types of wisdom cannot illuminate the true mechanism;
the traces [of practice] vary in depth, and the three beasts [of the sūtra] cannot reach its ultimate limit. Thus, "form is non-form" takes formlessness as its source;
"emptiness is non-emptiness" requires emptiness to dispel form. Therefore, we know that the ultimate voidness is imageless, yet it gives rise to all images.
This is the source of all things. The wondrous principle is beyond words; indeed, it is the root of all speech. This is because images arise from the imageless, and words arise from the wordless.
That which is wordless yet speaks does so because words are born in response to objects; that which is imageless yet appears as an image...
It is also because of the mind that images manifest; for though there are no words, they are spoken through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

Because there are no forms, the six-foot [Buddha] manifests his traces. Thus, this *Heart Sūtra* is the precious vehicle of the five modes of transport (*pañcayāna*), perfecting equality by adorning it with ten thousand virtues.
It is the sublime Mount Meru of the eight scriptural collections (*aṣṭapiṭaka*), standing alone in its splendor as it is embellished by the four treasures. It begins by extolling *prajñā*...

Regarding these "elements" (*dharma*), there were three interpretations in ancient times, but now there are five. First is the true aspect (*lakṣaṇa*), which refers to ultimate truth. Second is contemplative illumination (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), which refers to true wisdom.

Third is words and letters (*vyañjana*), which refers to the true teaching. Fourth is the objective realm (*viṣaya*), which refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*). Fifth is the retinue (*parivāra*), which refers to the myriad practices (*sarva-caryā*).

One must necessarily cultivate both merit and wisdom together; emptiness and existence must be illuminated in equal measure. By investigating the expressions to exhaust their underlying intent, one may realize the meaning through understanding.
The nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the resources of wisdom are both termed *prajñā*. *Pāra* means "the other shore" and "transcendence. *Mi* means "to reach.

By practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one transcends all obscurations and defilements; the objective realm is exhausted of both existence and non-existence; the meaning penetrates both the ultimate and the conventional;
awakening is fulfilled and tranquility is perfected—this is ascending to the other shore. *Prajñā* is the general name for the Great Sūtra. Mind...

"Zhe" (The One) is an alternative title for this sutra. "Jing" (Sutra) means that which is eternal and the Dharma; it is that which gathers and that which contemplates. Being eternal, its Way surpasses that of a hundred kings;
as the Dharma, it serves as a model for a thousand undertakings. To "gather" is to collect these wondrous principles; to "contemplate" is to awaken those myriad sentient beings.
It is intended that they may surely leave the ford of suffering and ultimately ascend to the shore of enlightenment. "One fascicle" (yī juàn) means that the beginning and the roll are not two.
It is named "One. Its opening and closing, its contraction and expansion, are designated as a "fascicle" (*juan*). Therefore, it is called *The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom*, One Fascicle.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound perfection of wisdom...

This sutra contains only the main body (*saddharma*), the introduction (*nidāna*), and the dissemination (*parīndanā*). It appears at the beginning and end of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin jing).

Specifically, the following chapter extensively elucidates the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), as well as the arising and ceasing of emptiness and form, and their defilement, purity, increase, and decrease.
Its form is like that of a tortoise’s hair; it exists only as words, yet has no actual appearance. Even the objects and contemplations of the Three Vehicles are but emptiness.

If one departs from delusion, then the Four Noble Truths of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās are the dharmas upon which one rides.
The Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas are the persons who ride them. If there were...

The one who is able to ride [the vehicle] has not yet abandoned the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*); seeing that there is a vehicle to be ridden, the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persists.
If neither the person nor the phenomena have been eliminated, this is merely the conceptual calculation of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*); how could it be called a Bodhisattva?

It is like a person who, while asleep, dreams of riding a boat across a river and reaching the other shore; suddenly waking up, they find themselves originally in their own place—the river and the boat having vanished.

Both [the person and the phenomena] are unreal. When a Bodhisattva cultivates the path and realizes that both persons and phenomena are empty, they enter the seventh stage and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Looking back upon the vehicle and that which is carried by it, they see them as being like a dream or an illusion; this is the true Bodhisattva.
Relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, they realize that both characteristics and views are empty, and both obstacles are exhausted. And...
They attain nirvāṇa. For this reason, the Buddhas of the three periods of time are cited as witnesses;
all have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by relying upon the *prajñāpāramitā*. Thus, the benefit of the teachings of this sūtra is vast and great.
Desiring to cause sentient beings to practice and disseminate it, I shall now provide a brief analysis of this sūtra according to ten topical sections (*daśamukha*) prior to its explanation.

1. The First [Chapter]. 2. The Second: The Section on the Arising of Conditions for Entering the Gate of Contemplation. 3. The Third: The Section on Realizing the Emptiness and Pervasive Penetration of the Aggregates to Cross Over Calamities.
4. The Fourth: The Section on the Non-duality of Emptiness and Form as Being One Suchness. 5. The Fifth: The Section on Defilement and Purity Being Only Reality and Lacking Falsehood.
6. The Sixth: The Section on the Twelve Bases Being Like Illusions. 7. The Seventh: The Section on the Three Bases Having Identical Substance but Different Names.
Seventh: The Section on the Emptiness of Both Object and Contemplation in the Three Vehicles; Eighth: The Section on Manifesting Emptiness through Excellence and Freedom from Obstructions;
Ninth: The Section on the Great Wisdom Vehicle’s Cause Leading to the Fruit; Tenth: The Section on the Divine Mantra for Protecting Difficulties and Promoting Circulation.
This sutra is complete with the three vehicles; its words and meaning are profound and subtle. If one receives, maintains, reads, and recites it, one shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

The inconceivability of name and teaching: [the Bodhisattva] is neither born nor extinguished, and even where there is no wisdom and nothing to be attained, all are in accord with the wondrous essence of True Suchness (tathatā).

This is called the inconceivability of principle. That is to say, he gives rise to compassion and wisdom, practicing both the ultimate and conventional truths simultaneously, and is not constrained by either nirvana or saṃsāra;
for this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. This is called the inconceivability of practice.

Being able to employ wisdom to transcend the two obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as all forms of grasping, one attains the two sublime fruits of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* through the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of results;
this is termed the "inconceivability of the fruit. These constitute the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit.
It is not that which the mind can conceive; it transcends the sphere of mental measurement (*cittamātra*). It is not that which the mouth can discuss; it lies beyond all verbal expression.
This teaching, its principle, its practice, and its fruit—therefore, they are all termed "inconceivable" (*acintya*).

Within the preceding section on the arising of images during the gate of contemplation, the text is divided into two parts: first, the practitioner who performs the practice is identified; second, the dharma to be practiced is elucidated. If...
First, the practitioner who performs the practice is identified; this is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Next, the dharma that is practiced is clarified; this is the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Within the Prajñāpāramitā, it is divided into three sections. The first is the letter.
The first is called "shallow prajñā. The second, which gives rise to wisdom based on the text, is called "middling prajñā.
The third, which clearly perceives that the essence of the five aggregates is empty, is called "deep prajñā. The first is the subject that illuminates, and is thus named deep prajñā;

the second is the object illuminated, namely the dharmas such as the five aggregates. Within these five aggregates, the first is the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*), consisting of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion. The second...
Regarding the mental factors—feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness—it next clarifies that both the objects of emptiness and form are unreal.
It further clarifies that arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, and increase and decrease each lack intrinsic nature.

Finally, it clarifies that the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and even the objects and contemplations of the three vehicles are all empty; there is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance, and thus there is no middle vehicle.
The object of contemplation is without old age and death, nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death; thus, there is no person of the Middle Vehicle who can contemplate it.

There is no suffering or its origin, which means there is no object for the Small Vehicle. There is no cessation or the path, which means there is no wisdom of the Small Vehicle that can contemplate it.
There is neither wisdom nor attainment, which means there is no object contemplated by the Great Vehicle. Because there is nothing to be attained.
Thus, there is no Mahāyāna wisdom capable of contemplation. "Contemplation" refers to *prajñā* (wisdom).

That which is able to perceive the principle of the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena is precisely the simultaneous relinquishing of both existence and non-existence, the mutual forgetting of both medicine and disease, and the non-reliance upon signs.

It involves subsuming objects within the mind until both mind and object are extinguished, leaving no dualistic marks, being like empty space. To perceive this essential nature of reality is called [the realization of the ultimate].
Attaining mastery: by contemplating that the mind of greed is illusory, one attains mastery within the gateway of giving (*dāna*);

by contemplating that the nature of transgression is empty and quiescent, one attains mastery within the gateway of ethical discipline (*śīla*); by contemplating that even the nature of ignorance is empty, one attains mastery within the gateway of wisdom (*prajñā*);
and by contemplating the provisional teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, one [attains mastery] within the gateway of the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*).
One attains mastery. Contemplating the gradual teaching of the Middle Vehicle, one attains mastery within the twelve links of dependent origination.
Contemplating the Mahāyāna’s freedom from attachment, one attains mastery within the gates of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. Contemplating the emptiness of form, there is mastery of the eye;
contemplating the emptiness of sound, there is mastery of the ear; and so on, up to the emptiness of phenomena and space, there is mastery of the mind. Thus one is able to contemplate.
The emptiness of mind is internal mastery; that the objects of observation are unreal is external mastery.

Since not a single dharma can be apprehended internally or externally, it is therefore called "mastery. If a practitioner does not employ wisdom to contemplate the emptiness of all dharmas, a攀緣心 (攀緣心;

*pān-yuán-xīn*; grasping and clinging mind) will arise. Because this mind arises, one takes up sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and engages in karma, which creates an obstruction. This obstruction hinders the Noble Path.

They are not called "sovereign," but rather are bound by the fetters of affliction: the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of false conceptualization, the fetter of names and signs, and the fetters of all afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion.
All sentient beings, dwelling within the five aggregates, undergo the injustice of saṃsāra through the twenty-five states of existence;
they circulate back and forth, passing through the three miserable realms, and endure all manner of suffering. They are not called "sovereign. If one relies upon...
Having previously developed wisdom, one realizes that both persons and phenomena are empty; thus, the two obstructions—the afflictive and the cognitive—are both exhausted.
This stage of practice is called "Mastery. Regarding *bodhisattva*: in the language of the West (Sanskrit), *bodhi* means "enlightenment" (*mārga*), and *sattva* means "sentient being" (*sattva*).
This refers to sentient beings who possess the mind of the Way (*bodhicitta*). As for "the Way" (*mārga*), it means the thorough penetration of principles and meanings.

"Thorough" (*tong*) signifies pervasive openness; "penetration" (*da*) signifies clear realization. When one is pervasively open and thoroughly realized, both mind and objects are empty, and there is no obstruction.
For example, in the world, a path that has thorny thickets, forests, pits, or ditches obstructs people's coming and going and is not called a "path. [The same applies to] the Bodhisattva...
If one perceives external objects as existing apart from the mind and thereby gives rise to greed and hatred, the six perfections will not be realized and all things will be obstructed;
this is likewise not called the Way. *Bodhi* refers to wisdom (*jñāna*), and *sattva* refers to a person. A person who possesses wisdom is called a *bodhisattva*.
*Bodhi* denotes insight (*prajñā*), and *sattva* denotes a person. Wisdom is able to discern that existence is itself non-existence, while insight is able to penetrate emptiness.
That is precisely the absence of emptiness. To have emptiness and yet possess [the capacity] to dispel it is what is called wisdom (*prajñā*). One who possesses wisdom is called a *bodhisattva*.
Now, taking the term *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *sattva* (being), if one explains the meaning briefly, they are called a "Bodhisattva.
Question: Up until now, all the virtuous ones have said that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is Guanshiyin. This...
Question: How is this explained? Answer: It is said that "this is what is given" and "this is what is given.

All Bodhisattvas likewise enter the first stage (*bhūmi*), where the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are exhausted. Having entered the fourth stage, attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) also ceases. With the twofold emptiness of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), they realize the object and the subject simultaneously;
compassion and wisdom are established together, and the ultimate and conventional truths are practiced in tandem. Because they possess compassion, they constantly abide in *nirvāṇa*.
He does not stagnate in emptiness because he possesses wisdom; he dwells perpetually within birth and death yet is undefiled by afflictions.
He is not obstructed by the two dharmas of affliction and nirvana. Since all bodhisattvas have attained mastery, why should Avalokiteśvara alone be called "Mastery" (Īśvara)?

One who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* employs applied effort and, by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), illuminates the six sense organs, the six consciousnesses, the six objects, the five aggregates (*skandha*), and the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Contemplating the mind without interruption, they remain in accord with the principle.
"Progressing from moment to moment" is like a person traveling a long distance: if their feet do not stop, they will reach their destination.

When a Bodhisattva practices the various perfections (pāramitās) on the path, their mind remains uninterrupted, enabling them to attain the fruit of Buddhahood; for this reason, it is called "practice. As for "profound":
Having realized that both person and phenomena are empty, one simultaneously casts off both form and mind;

with both object and contemplation extinguished, one transcends the realm of mental measurement and departs from the sphere of verbal expression. It is not what can be proclaimed by the mouth, nor what can be fathomed by the mind;
it is not the domain of the Two Vehicles, but is known only by Buddha and Buddha—therefore, it is called "profound. As for *prajñā*, the prefix *pra-* has two [meanings].
The meaning [of *artha*] is twofold: first, the meaning of purity; second, the meaning of supreme excellence. To be forever free from turbidity is called "pure" (*śuci*).

To be far removed from dust and free from defilement is called "pure" (*viśuddha*). To be beyond all comparison and peerless is called "supreme" (*praṇīta*). That which cannot be fathomed by mind or speech is termed "wondrous" (*prabhāsvara*). If one encompasses both meanings, there are two aspects:
first, wisdom (*jñāna*); second, discernment (*prajñā*). Wisdom is like the sun; it is the fundamental essence. Discernment is like its light; it is the arising of function.

Because it expresses both essence and function, it is called "wisdom" (prajñā). To perceive persons or phenomena is itself deluded thought; to be able to realize that both persons and phenomena are empty is what is called wisdom.
To give rise to thoughts and stir the mind, to perceive existence or non-existence, or to perceive the mind or its objects—these are all delusions.

To perceive emptiness and perceive form, to perceive "is" and perceive "is not," and to perceive all phenomena as existing externally to the mind—creating such dualistic distinctions—is in every case mere deluded conceptualization.
To thoroughly understand that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and fundamentally unceasing is true realization.

There are no two characteristics; it is like empty space. To perceive this essential nature is called wisdom (*prajñā*). The term *pāra* has two meanings: first, the meaning of "this shore" (*apāra*);

second, the meaning of "the other shore" (*pāra*). Regarding "this shore": first, it refers to the birth-and-death of fragmentation (*pariccheda-śarīra-jāti-maraṇa*), which is the "this shore" of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
second, it refers to the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāma-śarīra-jāti-maraṇa*), which is the "this shore" of Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage.
The Shore. There are five meanings of "the other shore" (*pāra*): first, the shore of teaching; second, the shore of principle; third, the shore of the object; fourth, the shore of practice;

and fifth, the shore of fruition. Regarding the shore of teaching: the textual characteristics of this sutra are able to serve as a raft for the dharma of the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇadharma*);
thus it is called the shore of teaching. Relying upon this teaching, one uses the raft to attain the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena.
The wondrous principle is called the "other shore of principle. Constantly contemplating this principle without interruption in the mind is called the "other shore of the object.

To simultaneously abandon the two attachments—namely, the attachment to a self and the attachment to phenomena—and to simultaneously abandon the two types of death—namely, the death of fragmentation and the death of transformation—and to simultaneously eliminate the two obstacles—namely, the obstacle of afflictions and the obstacle to the known—and to simultaneously realize the two kinds of emptiness—namely...
The emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena constitute the dual cultivation of two practices: namely, the practice for one’s own benefit and the practice for the benefit of others.

The practice for one’s own benefit employs wisdom (*prajñā*), while the practice for the benefit of others employs compassion (*karuṇā*). The simultaneous application of both compassion and wisdom is called the "perfection of practice" (*caryā-pāramitā*).

By practicing in this manner, one attains the sublime fruit of Bodhi; this is called the "perfection of the fruit" (*phala-pāramitā*). The term *pāramitā* has two meanings: first, "departure," and second, "arrival."
"Detached" means detached from all mental constructs (*cittamātra*) as well as from words and language. "Arrived" means arrived at the principle of the true mark of suchness (*tathatā*).
Question: Birth-and-death is this shore, and nirvāṇa is the other shore. I do not yet understand what the essential nature of that which lies between them is.
Answer: If one is detached from change (*pariṇāma*) but has not yet reached nirvāṇa, that which lies between these two is called "inferior."

Although the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) have not yet been completely extinguished, they cannot cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms because their residual impressions (*vāsanā*) are weak;
thus they are called "inferior untainted seeds" (*hīnānāsrava-bīja*). Since they are neither of the two extremes, they are also termed the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
As for "time," it refers to the moment of awakening and entry, like a thousand-year-old dark room suddenly illuminated by a bright lamp.

In the realm of darkness, however, there is none. Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been obscured and obstructed by afflictions, performing various karmic actions that permeate their consciousness and bring about immeasurable seeds for the three miserable realms.
If one turns back the light of wisdom, within a single thought-moment, all karmic obstructions will be entirely extinguished. By applying the mind to observe, [the afflictions...]
Because it is the time when affliction is extinguished, it is called "time. Question: One may designate the mind that discerns and contemplates as *prajñā*.
However, both words and the true nature (*dharmatā*) are not themselves acts of contemplative observation; how can they be equally termed *prajñā*? Answer:

If there were no words, by what means would sentient beings achieve awakening and understanding? It is necessary to rely on the chisel of speech before one can attain awakening and illumination. Therefore, words are designated as [such].
Prajñā must rely upon awakening-illumination; this illumination reaches the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). The illuminating subject and the illuminated object are of one essence and are unified.
For this reason, the true mark is also called prajñā. Thus, the Treatise says: "That which is called wisdom and the locus of wisdom are both termed prajñā.
Wisdom is indeed prajñā; the "locus of wisdom" is that which is illuminated, namely, the true mark. Therefore...
All three stages are likewise termed *prajñā*. The verse says:
Although the Hīnayāna has realized the selflessness of persons, The delusion of clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) remains unaltered;
Thus, it cannot master both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra. The Bodhisattva, however, attains mastery therein.
What has been explained thus far, although it involves the distinction between the subject that contemplates and the object contemplated within the three types of *prajñā*,
generally clarifies the section on the causal origination of entering the gate of contemplation for the first time.
To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty is to transcend all suffering and calamity.
"Perception" refers to wisdom. It is like a lamp illuminating the darkness: when the lamp arrives, the darkness is extinguished; when wisdom arises, ignorance is exhausted.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). That which possesses substantial resistance is called form; that which experiences is feeling; that which grasps characteristics is perception;
that which performs volitional activity is mental formation; and that which discerns is called consciousness. "Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of accumulation.

By accumulating form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one constitutes a body. This applies equally to those in the three realms and the four modes of birth, all of which share a single substance, each arising from the past.

With ignorance, karma, and grasping as causes, they perfume and form the distinctions of wholesome and unwholesome retributions. Yet this ignorance and karma result in the suffering of craving for one's home;
whether born in the heavens or among humans, there is the suffering of poverty and hardship, and the suffering of separation from those one loves.

The suffering of association with the loathed, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death—all arise based upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
From the eight sufferings down to the three sufferings, there is no birth within the three realms that is not suffering.
If one can thoroughly comprehend that the five aggregates are entirely illusory, one should contemplate form as being like a mass of foam, sensation as being like bubbles on water, and perception...
Like the heat of a spring mirage, all conditioned phenomena are like the plantain tree; contemplate consciousness as an illusion.
Within the two types of selflessness, their essential nature is found to be unattainable; all that is spoken of is empty. If the five aggregates were real, the eightfold suffering would not be false.
When the five aggregates are realized as empty, upon what could the eight sufferings depend? It is like a violent wind striking the water to form bubbles:

those bubbles are not the water, yet when the bubbles disperse, they become water; that water is not the bubbles. Bubbles are a metaphor for sentient beings, and water is a metaphor for Buddha-nature.
When the True is struck to produce the delusory, it is called "sentient beings"; when delusion is understood, it is called "True. Thus, suffering has no place of arising. Therefore, it is said:
"Clearly seeing that the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends all suffering and calamity. Question: "In the three realms there is the aggregate of form;
since the aggregate of form exists, one may speak of suffering and calamity. However, in the formless realm there is no aggregate of form; therefore, there ought to be no eightfold suffering there."
The answer is: Although there is no coarse form within the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), subtle form still persists.
When the World-Honored One entered *nirvāṇa*, the devas of the Formless Realm shed tears like a fine rain. If they possessed no form, from where would these tears come?

Since subtle form has not yet perished, the seeds of consciousness remain. Although they dwell in the eight meditative attainments (*aṣṭasamāpatti*), the signs of perception have not yet been eliminated; thus, they continue to circulate in the cycle of coming and going.
One is freed from the eight sufferings. The verse says:
The four elements and five aggregates are all non-material; The self, the person, and sentient beings are empty by nature.
If one can give rise to wisdom and illuminate with the mind, One will forever bid farewell to suffering and emerge from the cage of affliction.
As previously set forth, that which illuminates and that which is illuminated—the five aggregates of form and mind—are distinct and different.
This concludes the second section, "The Manifestation of the Emptiness of the Aggregates and the Crossing Over of Calamities."
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Form (*rūpa*) refers to shape and color. Solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is that which is void and pervasive;

it is so called because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). When it is said that "form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form," this is addressed for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles who, in extinguishing form, grasp at emptiness, yet do not realize that emptiness is their own mind.
Because they perceive an external realm of emptiness apart from the mind, their minds are obstructed by the perceived objects, and the objects are obstructed by the perceiving mind.

This is precisely what is called form; therefore, it is said that emptiness is not different from form. As for "form itself is emptiness," the Bodhisattva thoroughly realizes that the nature of form is inherently empty.
It is not that form ceases to exist before it is empty; it is not that the absence of form is called emptiness; it is not that it is empty because of contemplative observation;

it is not that it is empty because the mind has been exhausted; nor is it empty because phenomena have been dismantled. It is like the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise—fundamentally [non-existent].

Because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is said that form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. If one perceives emptiness as being outside the mind, one is once again obstructed by emptiness;
therefore, it is said that emptiness is itself form. Emptiness is not empty of itself; it exists because of form. Form is not form of itself;
it exists because of emptiness. Through emptiness one knows that form exists, and through form one knows that [emptiness] exists.
Emptiness. Apart from emptiness there is no separate form; apart from form there is no separate emptiness. At times the Buddhas speak of form, and at times they speak of the formless.
Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither form nor non-form. Emptiness is also like this. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The mind can exhaustively perceive form; when form is exhausted, it is not the mind. Apart from the mind there is no exhaustive form; apart from the exhaustive [form]..."
Form is without mind. All things that exist in mutual dependence are to be understood according to this principle.

For example, suppose there are two people with impaired vision traveling alone along a road; on both sides of the path, there are deep pits. Not seeing them, they may fall to the east of the road or to the west.
As they are about to fall into a pit and cannot see the correct path, they encounter a person who leads them toward the middle way.
All sentient beings are likewise thus: their eye of wisdom is obscured by various afflictions, leading them to falsely cling to emptiness and cling to form.

When they hear it said that "form is not different from emptiness," they immediately grasp at emptiness as being existent; when it is said for them that "emptiness is not different from form," [they likewise misapprehend].
If one clings to form as being real, I teach that form is itself emptiness. If one then clings to emptiness as being truly existent, I teach that emptiness is itself form.
Yet, the clinging to form still arises and is not eliminated; one ultimately merely chases after words and pursues sounds, for the mind has not yet been fully dispelled.
Now, by means of four stages, I overturn the relationship between mind and objects until the source is finally exhausted. It is like a person who...

Those whose two eyes are both squinting are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), whose wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) has not yet opened and who do not see that the Middle Way is right.

Those who face deep pits on both sides are those who cling to annihilationism or eternalism, cling to emptiness or form, and constantly give rise to the evil views of the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
The one person encountered on the road is none other than the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, who instruct them to avoid the deep pits.
It is one who, having abandoned the evil views of the two extremes, explains the correct path to enlightenment. As for emptiness and form, both are transformations of one’s own mind.
Because one realizes that the mind and its objects are non-dual, it is said that "form is not different from emptiness.

That "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise" refers to the mental factors (*caitta*). Since form has already been analyzed through four inversions, [the same applies to] the mind...
The Dharma is not different from form; it is omitted for brevity, hence it is said, "it is likewise so. The verse says: Emptiness and form are mutually dependent;
how could they ever be real? Within them there is only the single True Suchness (tathatā).
When the mind and its objects are clearly understood to be like illusions and dreams, One wanders freely, entering alone into the state of Nirvana without remainder.
The emptiness and form previously cited differ in four successive layers of inversion; together they clarify that the third [point], emptiness and form being as one, is without two parts.
Śāriputra, this mark of the emptiness of all dharmas is neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This refutes the dualistic marks of arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease. Śāriputra is named "Son of Śārī" because his mother’s name was Śārī;
he received this name from his mother, hence he is called Śāriputra. As for the mark of emptiness of all dharmas:

categories such as the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are empty in both essence and characteristic; therefore, they are called the mark of emptiness. Non-arising...

Regarding "non-extinction": if one perceives that all phenomena have arising, then there is the extinction of phenomena. Since phenomena are fundamentally without arising, how could there be the extinction of phenomena?
It is like a person with cataracts who falsely sees flowers in the sky; these very flowers in the sky are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature.
It is merely due to deluded conceptualization that the eye of wisdom is obscured. Upon the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one gives rise to a deluded mind that perceives arising and ceasing.

If the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) were existent, then because they are said to exist, one could speak of their arising. Yet, when one thoroughly realizes that the five aggregates are empty, how can there be arising within emptiness?
If the five aggregates were subject to arising, then because they are said to arise, one could speak of their ceasing. However, the five aggregates are fundamentally non-existent.
If there is no arising, how could there be cessation? Therefore, it is said to be "neither arising nor ceasing. Regarding "neither defiled nor pure":

when ordinary beings have not yet eliminated their afflictions (*kleśa*), and greed and hatred are present, they give rise to the notions of self and person and thereby cling; this is called "defilement.

When those of the Two Vehicles have exhausted their afflictions, having suppressed and departed from greed and hatred, they realize the emptiness of persons; this is termed "purity. If there were such defilement...
It can be removed; that is to say, there is something removable that may be designated as "pure. Yet, when one investigates the essence of defilement, it is fundamentally empty.

Within this very emptiness, how could there be purity? Therefore, it is said to be neither defiled nor pure. As for "neither increasing nor decreasing," this refers to the essential nature of the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
Sinking into the six realms of existence does not necessarily involve a decrease [in essence], and emerging from the three worlds does not necessarily involve an increase.

While it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* when enmeshed in defilements and the *dharmakāya* when free from them, although these terms for entering and exiting differ, the true nature of reality (*tathatā*) is fundamentally without distinction.
Taking the dharma-nature as its body, it is without obstruction, just like space, which has no...
[If one were to say there is form, etc.,] it would be a diminution. Therefore, in emptiness there is no form; there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
This is a repeated refutation of the two dharmas of form and mind, citing all five aggregates equally as empty; [this is done] for fear that [the reader] might not understand this.
Reiterating that if form and mind lack intrinsic nature, it is said: "Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. The verse says:
"Arising and ceasing, empty space, and the conditioned mind’s attachment; Pure consciousness is contrary, and dualistic consciousness does not pass through."
To know increase and decrease as being without benefit or harm is to be identical with the *dharmatā* of the Muni;
this section generally clarifies the fourth distinction, that of defilement and purity, which is solely reality and devoid of delusion.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomenon.

This is the refutation of the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Like an illusion produced by conditions, they have no reality. "There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind" refers to the emptiness of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).

How are they empty? Within the eye, the skin and flesh constitute the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*); the moisture is the water element (*abdhātu*); [the heat is] the fire element (*tejodhātu*); and... the eye.
Tears constitute the water element; the nature of warmth constitutes the fire element; movement constitutes the wind element. Question: Is earth the eye? Answer:
Earth is not the eye. Question: Is water the eye? Answer: Water is not the eye. Question: Is fire the eye? Answer: Fire is not the eye.
This fire is not the eye. Is wind the eye? This wind is not the eye. The four great elements are each distinct; this is called their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

When they combine to form the eye-faculty, this is called its suffering characteristic (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*). Before the four great elements exist, there is no eye-faculty with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Once the four great elements exist, there is no eye-faculty with extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*). Being neither self-natured nor other-natured, it is precisely the eye-faculty.
Emptiness. Since the nature of the eye is empty, there is also no such thing as "no-eye. The same applies to the following five faculties. As for the absence of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch:

if the six faculties were real, the six objects they correspond to would not be void. Since one finds through investigation that the six faculties are empty, it is clear that the six objects they correspond to do not exist.
How, then, can they be called "faculties" (indriya)? They are so named because they are able to produce [cognition].
Because it is consciousness. Why is it called "dust" (*rajas*)? Because it can defile and stain the pure mind. The four dusts form the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
the four great elements form the various sense faculties (*indriya*). As the various sense faculties encounter the six objects (*viṣaya*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are established.

Each arises from conditions; this clarifies that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Question: Previously, you mentioned the five aggregates (*skandha*), or the twelve bases and eighteen elements (*dhātu*). Now...
What is the distinction between these three characteristics? The answer is: For example, it is like a bird-catcher who, having caught a bird, relies on a single eye to keep it still;

yet one cannot use that single eye as a net. Similarly, while one may rely on the single dharma of *prajñā* (wisdom) to realize sainthood after understanding the mundane, one cannot teach others using that single dharma alone, because there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of faculties and the depth or shallowness of realization.

Profound. For this reason, the World-Honored One, guiding beings according to their capacities, employs various skillful means to teach the dharma-gates of the three categories, enabling them all to awaken and enter therein. The verse says:
Hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion constitute the fundamental [elements]; like an illusion, they cause birth and death to momentarily pause.
Although the internal and external dual extremes exist as opposites, when one contemplates their essential nature, they are like a city of Gandharvas.
The sense organs and objects previously cited differ between the two locations; this collectively clarifies the fifty-second entry among the bases (*āyatana*).
The section on illusion:
"There is no eye-element, up to and including no mind-consciousness-element.

This refutes the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). Having previously cited the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), both of which are empty in two locations, this clarifies the six [consciousnesses] in between.
Consciousnesses each lack intrinsic nature. Because there are sense bases (indriya) and objects (viṣaya), the six consciousnesses arise. How do they arise? The answer is:

because there is the object-form (rūpa-viṣaya), the eye-base arises and visual consciousness is produced; because there is the object-sound (śabda-viṣaya), the ear-base arises and auditory consciousness is produced; and so on, up to:
because there is the object-phenomena (dharma-viṣaya), the mind-base arises and mental consciousness is produced. This occurs because one does not realize the [nature of] the objects. Thus...
Delusive thoughts arise; they can serve as the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Re-entering the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), they form the seeds for the immeasurable three realms and four modes of birth, causing one to cycle through the six destinies without end. Why are these called afflictions?

As well as greed, hatred, and delusion. The answer is: when the eye conditions visible forms, it is called "affliction" (*paryavasthāna*); when visible forms come into contact with the eye, it is termed "distress" (*upāyāsa*).

When the six consciousnesses condition the six sense objects, it is called "affliction"; when the six sense objects come into contact with the six consciousnesses, it is termed "distress. Regarding greed, hatred, and delusion:
because the eye conditions visible forms, one feels desire for pleasant forms and aversion toward unpleasant forms.
To discriminate between the good and the evil is called delusion (*moha*). The attachment of various afflictions within the two faculties should be understood accordingly. Question:
What kind of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) must one perform to overcome these afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion? Answer:

If a practitioner can realize the mind and reflect inwardly, such that the essential nature of the faculties cannot be apprehended, this is called the Gate of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*). As for the objects of the senses...
This is false and illusory; it is precisely the non-arising and non-ceasing of consciousness, which is the Gate of Wishlessness (*apraṇihita-mukha*).

Because there is neither non-existence nor existence within these three locations, they are called the Three Gates of Emptiness (*trīṇi śūnyatā-mukhāni*). Because these three locations are not bound, they are also called the Three Gates of Liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣa-mukhāni*).

Because one can penetrate the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ viṣayāḥ*), they are also called the Gates of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā-mukha*). Because all consciousnesses are merely quiescent and extinguished, they are also called the Gate of Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*).
When the six consciousnesses cease, there is no affliction; when the six sense objects are empty, there is no vexation.

Since sense objects are not real, one does not perceive any beautiful form to be craved, nor does one perceive any ugly form to be resented. With nothing to differentiate, the mind is free from delusion.
If one can accord with this principle, greed, hatred, and delusion will all be extinguished and afflictions will be forever exhausted; this is precisely what is called *nirvāṇa without remainder*.

As for the statement that there are no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, and no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas, and no visual faculty up to and including no mental consciousness faculty—this is intended to destroy the attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.

The eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu) refer to the meaning of differentiation. The six sense organs (ṣaḍindriya) take the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) as their conditions; because they are each distinct, they are called the eighteen elements.
When the eighteen elements are cited to refute the notion of a self (ātman), if there were a self within the eye, there should be none within the ear.
If there were a self within each individual sense-faculty and its corresponding object, then for a single person there would be eighteen selves in total.
If, however, there is no self within each individual sense-faculty and object, then the eighteen elements (dhātus) would not exist at all. Thus, one knows that the self has no substantial reality.
The eye conditions the object of form, the ear conditions the object of sound, and so on until the body conditions the object of touch; these constitute the sense-faculties.
The five sense objects are all visible. As for the nature of the mental consciousness that takes the dharma-object as its condition, how is it described?

The answer is: when the five faculties encounter the five sense objects, the five consciousnesses arise in between. Although the five faculties see, hear, perceive, and know, they cannot perform discrimination;
they must rely upon the simultaneous mental consciousness to discriminate such things as blue, yellow, red, white, square, round, dimensions, and so forth. This is called [discriminative perception].

Dharmas (mental objects). They function in the same way as the five consciousnesses, sharing the same objects as the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Among these five sense-objects, false conceptualization is termed "dharmas.
Question: The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of conceptualization; however, it is not yet clear what the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) functions to do.

Answer: The faculty of mind has the constant function of investigative deliberation (*tarka*). It possesses three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*) and four distinctions. Regarding the three types of perfuming:
There are four types: first, the perfuming of names and words; second, the perfuming of self-love; third, the perfuming of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*);
and fourth, the distinctions: first, the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*); second, self-love (*ātmasneha*); third, the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); and fourth, ignorance (*avidyā*).

These are constantly associated with the four afflictions and function as the seeds for all wholesome and unwholesome deeds. The five consciousnesses take the five sense objects as their external conditions, while the mental consciousness...

The consciousnesses that take the five sense objects as their common conditions also turn inward to take [internal objects] as conditions; this is called the nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The seven consciousnesses depend upon the six consciousnesses for their differentiation;
turning inward to take [objects] as conditions, they achieve the grasping of objects and the formation of seeds, subsequently re-entering the eighth consciousness.
That which exclusively takes the internal as its object is called "conditioned" (*ālambana*); this is the *paratantra-svabhāva*. The essence of the eight consciousnesses is the *tathāgatagarbha*;

as the fundamental reality, it is also called the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*. When the sense-faculties and their respective consciousnesses perceive form, the mental consciousness subsequently engages in conceptual discrimination.

Visual consciousness ceases immediately. The seventh consciousness that clings to and sustains the body, as well as the mental consciousness, also cease. The eighth consciousness, which receives perfuming, and the seventh consciousness also cease.
If the practitioner can realize inward illumination within the mind, the eye does not take form-objects as its condition, and the mental consciousness has nothing to differentiate.

Upon entering the first stage (bhūmi), one transforms the mental consciousness into the wisdom of wondrous observation; the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness have nothing [further] to [differentiate].

Appropriation (*upādāna*). In the seventh stage, the seven consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). The eighth consciousness, which does not receive perfuming, is the Tathāgatagarbha.

When the eighth consciousness is purified and transformed, it becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); it also transforms the five sense-consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

Thus, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is Done is the wisdom of wondrous discernment that constitutes the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body), while the Wisdom of Equality constitutes the Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body).
Regarding the body: the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom constitutes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). By consolidating the eight consciousnesses, one forms the four wisdoms;

through these four wisdoms, one achieves the three bodies (*trikāya*). As for the previous statement that there are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind, this refers to the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

They are divided into the eighteen *dhātus*. One thoroughly realizes that form (*rūpa*) is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The mind conditioned by the three periods of time cannot be apprehended in either case;
this is because both form and mind are fundamentally empty. Thus, one knows that the eighteen bases (*āyatanas*) do not exist, being spoken of only from the perspective of delusion.
Yet, it is not that the three bases do not exist apart from the mind. If explained according to principle, they are all the single mind’s illusory transformation. The verse says:
The eighteen bases of internal, external, and intermediate [realms]— just as one says that rabbit horns have no form from the beginning—
the Great Sage, responding to capacities through skillful means, provisionally established empty names according to their functional applications.
The aforementioned distinctions among the three locations of sense organs, objects, and consciousness collectively clarify the essence of the sixth location.
It is the same name but different divisions.
There is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance, and so on, up to neither old age and death nor the exhaustion of old age and death.
This refutes the objective realm of the Middle Vehicle. One contemplates it as being like a phantom or a mirage; because its essential nature cannot be found upon investigation, it does not exist.
Ignorance (*avidyā*), birth, and old age and death constitute conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The exhaustion of ignorance and of birth and old age is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Ordinary beings lack wisdom; when they give rise to the mind and take objects as conditions, this is termed ignorance. The followers of the Two Vehicles lack compassion; they extinguish ignorance and enter *nirvāṇa*.
The Bodhisattva possesses great wisdom; both mind and objects vanish together. Because this is not the same as conventional truth, it is [ultimately] non-existent.
Regarding ignorance (*avidyā*): because he possesses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and acts to transform sentient beings, he does not enter the stream of *nirvāṇa*.
Alternatively, because he does not exhaust ignorance, it is said that there is "no exhaustion of ignorance. Because ordinary beings lack wisdom, they undergo birth, old age, and death;

however, when a Bodhisattva perceives that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all empty, there is then no old age or death. The followers of the Two Vehicles lack compassion; they extinguish their physical forms and annihilate their wisdom, reaching [an end].
[The Bodhisattva] turns back birth, old age, and death. Because the Bodhisattva possesses great compassion, in order to transform sentient beings, he engages in the same activities as they;
thus, he does not exhaust birth, old age, and death. Therefore it is said: "There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance," and so on, up to "no old age and death."
Nor is there the exhaustion of old age and death. Regarding "ignorance" (*avidyā*): due to the absence of the light of wisdom, one performs various volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

"Formations" refers to unwholesome actions, meritorious actions, and immovable actions. Unwholesome actions such as killing, stealing, and other dharmas of false views are called "unwholesome actions."
Venerating the Buddha, reciting sutras, practicing giving, and observing the precepts are called meritorious conduct (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).
Sitting in meditation to attain the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, thereby subduing the mind so that it does not arise, is called immovable conduct (*āniñjyābhisaṃskāra*).

However, any wholesome or unwholesome karma performed by a practitioner—driven by a mind that fears the retribution of future results—is merely conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); it ultimately cannot escape the cycle of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Within the three realms and six paths of existence, the seeds of various karmas are sown and perfumed within consciousness.
When one encounters the demonic armies of birth and death, the realm of the place of rebirth one craves appears before them.

Once their karmic life-span is exhausted, they receive an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) and, after seven times seven days have passed, enter the mother’s womb, where they mingle with the parents’ semen and blood, blending the red and white elements.
When its flesh has formed into a mass, this is termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), which consists of the four aggregates (*skandha*): sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the four [elements]: solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. This is termed the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*), namely: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

The awareness of cold and warmth, pain and pleasure, and so forth, is called "contact" (*sparśa*). Because there is already an experiencing [of these], it is designated as "sensation" (*vedanā*). [Therein,] one conceives love for the mother...
The father feels aversion; when the father’s semen is emitted, [the being] considers it its own—this is called *tṛṣṇā* (craving).
To be greedily attached to the preceding object is termed *upādāna* (clinging). The accomplishment of the four great elements is termed *bhava* (becoming).

Prior to the forty-nine days, as the various winds sequentially dissolve and [the being] departs from the mother’s womb, this is termed *jāti* (birth). When karma and life-force are entirely exhausted and the four great elements disperse, this is [death].
This is called death. This constitutes the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) belong to the past.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*)—these eight links are designated as the present while in the mother’s womb. Birth (*jāti*) and old age-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are designated as the future.
Ignorance and formations are the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka*); consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling [are the projected factors].
The seeds of the five fruits are what is projected. Through craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), these three present factors bring about future birth and death (*jāti-maraṇa*).
For those of the Middle Vehicle, when ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases, they no longer perform volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); thus, formations cease.
Because there are no formations, the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*) also ceases. Since consciousness has ceased, everything up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) ceases as well.
One immediately transcends the three realms and will not undergo further existence. This is like the sons who, riding upon the deer carts, emerge from the burning house.

The principle of the Middle Vehicle holds that because there is ignorance, there is the cessation of ignorance; because there is old age and death, there is the cessation of old age and death. However, the contemplation of Prajñā is not thus:
ignorance is fundamentally non-existent, and likewise, there is no arising of the cessation of ignorance. To investigate [further]:
In the end, nothing can be apprehended. There is likewise no exhaustion of old age and death;
there is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path.

This serves to refute the objects of the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna, observing that they all lack substantial reality because the perceived and the perceiver have not yet been extinguished. It causes [the practitioner] to...
One contemplates that the essence of the five aggregates is quiescent and thereby realizes the emptiness of the person. To illustrate cause and effect by means of these Four Noble Truths:

the two truths of origination and the path are the causes; the two truths of suffering and cessation are the effects. The two truths of suffering and origination are conventional; the two truths of cessation and the path are ultimate.
Phenomena such as the five aggregates are termed the fruit of suffering; ignorance, craving, and karma are the causes of origination; [cessation is]... extinction.
The exhaustion of birth and death is called the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth constitute the causes of the path. A question is asked:
All internal and external phenomena follow the principle that the cause precedes the effect; thus, one rides upon the cause to reach the fruit.

If this is the case, it would be logical to first explain the cause and subsequently explain the fruit. Yet, in this sutra, the fruit of suffering—the five aggregates—is explained first, followed by...

Regarding the cause of origination (*samudaya-hetu*): for what reason is this? Answer: Now, the World-Honored One teaches the Four Noble Truths because those of the Hīnayāna disposition are of inferior capacity and do not comprehend the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena.

If he were to first teach the cause of origination and subsequently speak of the fruit of suffering, ordinary beings, lacking the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajāti-jñāna*), would be unable to thoroughly understand past ignorance, craving, and karma. Therefore, he causes them to contemplate the present.
From the fruit, one knows the past cause: those who today have long lives came from having practiced non-killing in the past;
those who today have short lives came from killing in the past; those who today are wealthy and noble came from practicing generosity and maintaining the precepts in the past;
those who today are poor and lowly came from being stingy, greedy, and breaking the precepts in the past. Such is the nature of all causes and effects.

It is all like this. Now, by citing the fruit, one immediately understands the cause. For this reason, the five aggregates as the fruit of suffering are presented first, followed by the explanation of their cause.
If one knows that the five aggregates are suffering, then regarding these present fruits of suffering, one will not create the causes for their accumulation.
To extinguish the causes of accumulation, it is necessary to cultivate the Path. The Path consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Concentration and wisdom are equal. By means of the factors that assist the Path, because one upholds the precepts, the mind is able to become concentrated; because it is concentrated, one is able to give rise to wisdom.
When the three vehicles are fully realized, both cause and effect are extinguished. The total extinction of cause and effect is called Nirvana.

Because it leads ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to transcend [suffering], it is called the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*). Question: What is the difference between the Ultimate Truth and the Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*)? Answer:
While the three vehicles (*triyāna*) collectively contemplate the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) regarding their superficial and profound aspects, their insights and understandings differ.

Ordinary beings cling to the five aggregates as being real and become immersed in the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Through their craving for these six sense objects, they are bound to birth and death; oppressed by various sufferings, they transmigrate through the six [realms].

The Way is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). To sever birth and death and extinguish craving, yet with the grasping at signs not yet eliminated, one attains nirvana by reducing the body to ashes and extinguishing consciousness;
thus one emerges from the mundane net, and it is therefore called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). These are the Four Noble Truths.
To thoroughly realize that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty and that suffering has no place of arising is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.

To have false conceptualizations not arise, and to realize that ignorance, craving, and karma have never existed from the beginning, such that there is no accumulation through combination, is called the Noble Truth of the Origin.
Within the dharma of ultimate cessation, to thoroughly realize that all dharmas are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished is called the Noble Truth of Cessation.

The Truth: One is able to know that both person and phenomena are empty; both form and mind are cast aside; both object and contemplation are simultaneously stilled; and both object and wisdom are both extinguished.
Both the subject that perceives and the object perceived are unreal, lacking dual characteristics, just like empty space.

One who performs this contemplation is said to realize the Noble Truth of the Path. Question: Śāriputra, those who are followers of the Lesser Vehicle [realize] suffering, its origin, and its cessation...
The Way is the Hīnayāna vehicle; this [text] carries both the person and the dharma. From ignorance up to old age and death—this is the Middle Vehicle (Madhyamaka-yāna).
Why does it not mention the person of the Middle Vehicle? This is because it contains the dharma but lacks the person.
What is the reason for this? Answer: The Middle Vehicle is the Pratyekabuddha-yāna. "Pratyekabuddha" means "one awakened through conditions."
The Buddha’s word is "awakening. It is awakening to the fact that the five aggregates arise from conditions;

within each aggregate, one seeks its essential nature and finds it unobtainable, thereby realizing the emptiness of the person. One then completely severs all discriminative afflictions. By contemplating conditions, one awakens.
They are called Pratyekabuddhas. Born in worlds where no Buddha exists, they attain awakening by themselves without a teacher; they are also called Solitary Buddhas (*Pratyekabuddha*).
If they were to appear before a Buddha, they would be termed Arhats of superior faculties and could not be called Solitary Buddhas within that same world-system.
There are no two Buddhas. Although they differ in their greatness or smallness, to avoid confusing the title of "Buddha," they cannot be born in the same place at the same time.
When the World-Honored One first attained the Way, he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects in three revolutions for the five bhikṣus in the Deer Park.
The first was the turning that demonstrates the characteristics: "O bhikṣus, this is suffering; this is the origin; this is..."
Cessation. This is the path. Second, the turning toward exhortation: "O monks, this is suffering; you must know it. This is its origin;
you must abandon it. This is its cessation; you must realize it. This is the path; you must cultivate it. Third, the turning toward citation of authority:
"This is suffering; I have known it. This is its origin; I have abandoned it. This is its cessation; I have realized it..."
"It has been realized. This is the path; I have cultivated it. Having seen suffering and abandoned its origin, I have realized cessation and cultivated the path.
Thus, I have emerged from the three realms. It is like the sons who, riding upon goat-carts, escaped from the burning house and attained arhatship.
Therefore, a sutra says: 'For example, there was a person who led a multitude of people toward a mountain of jewels. The road was vast and remote.'"

At three hundred yojanas [from their destination], the multitude became weary and exhausted, and all desired to turn back. The leader, possessing many skillful means, conjured an illusory city as a temporary resting place to allow them to recover.
The path to Buddhahood is vast and remote; it requires passing through immeasurable kalpas and enduring long-term toil and suffering.

Unable to achieve it, he consequently gave rise to a mind of retreat. The World-Honored One then preached the Truths of Suffering, Accumulation, Cessation, and the Path, which are precisely the places where the practitioner finds rest.
As for the present statement that there is no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path: since suffering is fundamentally unarisen, what suffering could there be?
Knowing that the origin of suffering has no combination, what is there to be abandoned? Since cessation has nothing to cease, what is there to be realized?
The Path is fundamentally formless; what is there to be cultivated? If there were a person capable [of cultivation], then there would be a Path to be cultivated.

Since there is neither a person capable of cultivating nor a Path to be cultivated, then both person and dharma are empty. One realizes the principle of suchness (*tathatā*). It is like a person who...
One may dream of facing an enemy with whom one engages in a clash of white blades; or dream of men and women traveling far away, separated from their loved ones through parting;
or dream of losing wealth, property, or clothing while life itself does not perish;
or dream of being old and sick upon a bed, with the time of death drawing near, experiencing at that moment extraordinary grief and suffering. Upon waking from sleep, all these sufferings [vanish].
Originally non-existent. It is the same for all sentient beings:

since beginningless time, they have been obscured by ignorance and have slept through the long night, mired in the six states of dullness, falsely perceiving various sufferings. As soon as Prajñā (wisdom) shines upon them, both persons and phenomena are seen to be empty.
Since the body no longer exists, what suffering could there be? By showing that even the single Truth of Suffering is not real, one comes to know the [remaining] three truths.
It is not real; therefore, it is said that there is no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path. Question:

When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they sometimes proceed from the profound toward the shallow, and sometimes from the shallow toward the profound. Why is it that in preaching this sutra, you first speak of the Middle Vehicle, then the Small Vehicle, and finally the Great Vehicle?
Answer: The Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma always relies upon the two truths and always elucidates them.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Within the ultimate truth, all words and letters are transcended.
If the three vehicles were substantially real, then a sequence would exist based on that reality. Since the three vehicles are all unreal, how could there be a sequence for what is unreal?
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The first stage is the eighth; the tenth stage is the first. Why is this? Because nothing exists. There is.
What follows?
"There is neither ignorance nor attainment.

Because there is nothing to be attained, this serves to refute the attachment to the existence of a Mahāyāna mind. There is no ignorance, and no wisdom-virtue of enlightenment; there is no attainment.
Regarding the virtue of cessation in *nirvāṇa*: Question: Bodhi and *nirvāṇa* are the places where sentient beings take refuge.
While it may be believed that these are non-existent in the case of the minor fruits of the Two Vehicles, how can it be said that they do not exist in the ultimate fruit of the Mahāyāna?

Answer: Bodhi and *nirvāṇa* are things grasped as existent by the deluded mind of sentient beings. Once the deluded mind is dispelled, their essence transcends both existence and non-existence. It is merely...
One removes the illness, yet does not remove the Dharma; this is the wondrous essence of True Suchness (tathatā), which transcends both existence and non-existence.
The "illness" is merely the deluded conceptualization of the clinging mind of sentient beings. Thus, a sutra says: "There is no Śrāvaka vehicle, Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or Tathāgata vehicle.
As long as the mind continues to function, these various vehicles are not ultimate. If that mind were extinguished, [there would be no vehicles]."
As for the vehicle and the one who rides it, there is no establishment of vehicles; I speak of them as the One Vehicle.
If one says that nirvana exists, then attachment to dharmas has not yet been extinguished. If one clings to the existence of bodhi, then attachment to a self has not yet been exhausted.
Bodhi is the characteristic upon the essence; nirvana is the essence underlying the characteristic. The Dharma-eye of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is pure.
To see the essence while not seeing its characteristics is because the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-eye is not yet clear;

to see the characteristics while not seeing the essence is as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where it says that a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage perceives the dharma-nature as if looking through a thin silk veil.

Now, when it is said that "there is neither wisdom nor attainment," this simultaneously refutes the two attachments and simultaneously realizes the two emptinesses. To awaken to the quiescent nature of bodhi is precisely to eliminate the attachment to a person (*pudgala-grāha*). To understand...
The essence of *nirvāṇa* is suchness (*tathatā*); this is precisely the elimination of attachment to phenomena (*dharma*). Bodhi and *nirvāṇa* are the objects of contemplation;

because they are non-apprehendable (*anupalabdha*), they are themselves the signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) that contemplates them. Question: If one posits phenomena as the object and the person as the subject, then the phenomenon comes first and the person later.

If one relies on the phenomenon to practice, then the phenomenon comes first and the person later. Although there is this distinction of priority, [the relationship between] person and phenomenon must...
[The interlocutor] says: "If there were dharmas but no person, the dharmas would be empty. If there were a person but no dharmas, the learner would have nothing to rely upon.

If both person and dharma were absent, one would fall into the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Now, you say that both person and dharma are empty; how can this be the same as [treating them like] bricks and stones?

To store [this teaching] and provide a foundation for the wise, it decisively uproots deep doubts. He replied: "It is not that person and dharma do not exist; rather, they are called 'empty' [in the sense of being devoid of self-nature]."

Arising from a multitude of conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Like the moon reflected in water or an image in a mirror, their appearance exists while their substance is non-existent;

it is the same for both phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*). When one speaks of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is to eliminate the grasping at a self of the person (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*).

When one speaks of the non-existence of phenomena, it is to eliminate the mind that clings to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa-citta*). If these two minds of grasping are absent, what fault could there be in persons and phenomena? [Verse]
It is said:
"Luminosity and ignorance—these two characteristics are [empty]. To speak of abandoning suffering and severing the origin is the dharma of foolish ordinary people;
the nature of phenomena is empty and is not attained through wisdom. The provisional establishment of the three vehicles is likewise all non-existent."

Regarding the gradual sequence of the objects and contemplations of the three vehicles previously cited, there are differences between the Great and Small [Vehicles]. This generally clarifies the seventh section, wherein both object and contemplation are empty:
"Because the Bodhisattva relies on the Prajñāpāramitā, his mind is without hindrance; because he is without hindrance..."
There is no fear; one is far removed from the dream-like appearances of inversion and attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
A *bodhisattva* is a sentient being who possesses the mind of the Way (*bodhicitta*). *Prajñā* is wisdom;

*pāramitā* means "reaching the other shore. When the mind is without obstruction—because it is without obstruction—one relies on the preceding contemplation of the objects and views of the Three Vehicles.

All are empty. Bodhi and nirvāṇa are quiescent in both nature and appearance; the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are eternally empty in their essential nature, and therefore there is no hindrance.
"Because there is no hindrance" reiterates the preceding text. Through the contemplation of wisdom, one then realizes awakening.
"There is no fear" means one is not terrified by birth nor intimidated by death; therefore—
Regarding the phrase "there is no fear; far removed from delusion and dream-like thoughts, one attains ultimate nirvana":
to perceive phenomena as existing outside the mind is called *di* (delusion); to be unaware that these are produced by one's own mind is called *dao* (inversion).

It is like a person who, having mistakenly eaten datura, has its toxic vapors enter the heart, causing them to falsely perceive empty flowers, needles, and other such things, being unaware that [these are merely illusions].
Transformed by poison, the mind falsely perceives needles and flowers outside itself; throughout the day it gathers flowers and picks up needles without ceasing.
To one who has not eaten datura, seeing such a person gathering flowers and picking up needles would cause everyone to laugh in astonishment, crying out that they have gone mad.
All sentient beings are deluded regarding their own fundamental nature; they do not realize that the realms they perceive are transformations of their own minds.
Thus, one perceives differentiated objects as existing outside the mind and seeks those objects by means of the mind.
When the wise observe this, it is no different from a madman searching for a needle. Therefore, it is said that perceiving phenomena as being external to the mind is called "delusion" (*viparyāsa*);

failing to understand that they are produced by one's own mind is termed "inversion. As for "dream-like thoughts," these refer to performing good or evil deeds within the state of grasping at attainments.
Karma is called "dream. To differentiate between nirvana and saṃsāra as being distinct is called "perception.
The simultaneous relinquishing of names and signs is called "the ultimate. The mutual disappearance of mind and objects is called "nirvana. The verse says:
The *sattva* relies on emptiness and is without obstruction; employing wisdom to cultivate the truth, they reach ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
By distancing themselves from deluded thoughts and eliminating inversions, "truth" refers to withdrawing the mind inward to contemplate what has been previously raised:
that the Bodhisattvas are able to abandon that which is to be abandoned. By removing delusion and realizing truth, their distinctions differ; [this is] the general [principle].
This clarifies the eighth section, "Exalting the Superiority of the Illumination of Emptiness and its Freedom from Obstructions":
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The past, future, and present constitute the three periods of time. "Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*). Through self-awakening, one severs the attachment to persons;

through awakening others, one severs the attachment to phenomena. Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are unable to awaken themselves; those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are unable to awaken others; and Bodhisattvas are unable to bring awakening to full completion. Because he differs from ordinary beings, he awakens himself;
because he differs from those of the two vehicles, he awakens others; and because he differs from [lesser] Bodhisattvas, [he brings awakening to full completion].
Awakening is fulfilled. It is like awakening from a dream; it is like a lotus flower opening, unstained by impurity. When the two forms of delusive sleep are exhausted, one is called a Buddha.
This is all because of reliance upon the *prajñāpāramitā*; as explained previously, through this, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
